patterns: 是 joins two nouns: A is B. It does not go before adjectives.
不 negates habits, wishes, facts and descriptions.
没 says something did not happen or has not happened.
有 means A has or owns B.
The negative of 有 is always 没有, never 不有.
Put the place first, then 有, to say something exists there.
里|上|下|前面|后面|这儿|那儿 有
Adjectives act as predicates with no 是. 很 is the usual link and is often not a strong 'very'.
Add 吗 to a statement to make it a yes/no question. The word order stays the same.
Asks 'and what about this one?' after something has been said.
Saying the positive then the negative makes a yes/no question.
'What' stays where the answer would go; it does not move to the front.
'Who' stays in the position of the person being asked about.
'Where', usually after 在 or a verb of going.
'Which one' needs a measure word after 哪.
Asks 'how many' when the expected number is small.
Asks 'how many' or 'how much' with no size expectation; the measure word is optional.
的 links an owner or describer to a noun: A's B.
A number cannot sit directly before a noun; a measure word goes between them.
Use 两, not 二, for two of something.
'This' and 'that' also take a measure word before the noun.
在 as a verb says where something is.
The place where an action happens goes before the verb.
了 after a verb marks the action as completed.
了 at the end says the situation is new or has changed.
会 means a skill you have learned, and also 'will probably'.
能 means able to, or allowed to, in the circumstances.
想 before a verb is 'would like to'.
要 before a verb shows a firm intention or a need.
'Also' goes before the verb, never at the start of the sentence.
都 goes before the verb and refers back to everything named before it.
和 joins nouns. It does not join verbs or whole clauses.
Time words come near the front, before the verb.
'Too' or 'so': often an exclamation rather than a complaint.
'Don't', a little firmer or more formal than 别.
吧 softens a sentence into a suggestion or a guess.
Destinations follow 来 and 去 directly, with no word for 'to'.
Dates run from the largest unit to the smallest.
Asks someone's age, or how big something is.
Softens an action: do it briefly, just a moment.
Doubling a verb makes it brief and casual.
和/跟 + person + 一起 + verb
还 means 'still' or 'also' before a verb.
过 says you have had this experience at some point.
着 says a state or action continues.
Stresses that the action is under way right now.
在 before a verb means someone is doing it now.
A is more so than B. Do not add 很 before the adjective.
A is not as much so as B.
A 跟/和 B 一样
A and B are the same, optionally followed by the adjective they share.
Chinese often states both the cause and the result.
Although... still. Unlike English, both halves carry a link word.
If... then. 就 sits before the verb in the second clause.
Something is about to happen; 就要 can follow a stated time.
Two actions at the same time, by one person.
Spotlights when, where or how a past event happened, or states a firm judgement.
Describes how well or how an action is done.
A second word says what the action achieved.
Shows direction relative to the speaker.
Marks who the action is done for or to.
Marks who or what an attitude or action is directed at.
Distance from one place or time to another.
From A to B, in space or in time.
就 ties a result to what came before: then, right away, or sooner and easier than expected.
才 means only then: later or harder than expected, or only on that condition.
'Or' in a question that offers a choice.
'But' at the start of the second clause.
Asks how something is, or offers a suggestion: how about it?
How long, how far, how tall and so on.
How long the action lasts goes after the verb.
How many times something is done goes after the verb.
Describers come before the noun, joined by 的: the book I bought.
With no noun after it, 的 means 'the one that belongs to...': 这是我的 is 'this is mine'.
A little too, usually said of something unwelcome.
A bit more so, used for comparing or asking for a change.
May, or it is fine to.
Like doing something; no word for 'to' is needed.
A lets or makes B do something.
When or while; the clause comes first.
Before or after: these follow the event, the reverse of English.
Brings the object forward to say what was done to it. The verb needs a result or follow-up.
A has something done to it, often unwelcome.
Except for, or in addition to, depending on whether 都 or 也 follows.
As long as: the condition is enough.
Only if: nothing else will do.
The more A, the more B.
As far as someone is concerned; for them.
In order to; the goal usually comes first.
Every one, without exception; 都 usually stays.
A question word plus 都 means everything, everyone or everywhere.
什么|谁|哪儿|哪里 都|也
一点儿|一点 也|都 不|没
It looks, sounds or tastes as if; judging by the senses.
看起来|听起来|闻起来|吃起来
The action starts and carries on.
Says whether a result is possible: can or can't manage it.
Two direction words after a verb show path and viewpoint.
有时候|有时 .. 有时候|有时
The exact or rough gap goes after the adjective.
A 比 B 更/还 + adjective
Use 更 or 还 in a comparison, never 很.
Again, of something that already happened.
Again, of something yet to happen.
Always, often with a hint of annoyance.
Checks a guess: isn't that so?
No matter what; more spoken than 无论.
Since that is the case, then...
Not only... but also; more formal than 不但.
Even though, stating a fact that is accepted.
尽管 .. 但|但是|可是|还是|仍然|也|却
If; 的话 closes the condition and either word can be dropped.
Stresses that a negative runs against what you might think.
A rhetorical question: surely you don't mean...?
Presses a question: what on earth? in the end?
If not this, then that: one of the two.
Take A as B; a written frame.
A is not as good as B.
Whether; a written form of 是不是.
At the moment when; adds a formal frame around 的时候.
地 turns a description into an adverb before a verb.
